lessons.title: Human body and health
lessons.keyIdea: Organ systems work together: the heart pumps blood, the lungs bring in oxygen, and the digestive system breaks down food.

sections.heading: Circulation
sections.body: The heart pumps blood through arteries (away from the heart), tiny capillaries, and veins (back to the heart). Red blood cells carry oxygen to every cell.

sections.heading: Digestion
sections.body: Mouth (chewing, saliva) → oesophagus → stomach (acid and churning) → small intestine (digested food absorbed into blood) → large intestine (water absorbed).

sections.heading: Health
sections.body: A balanced diet includes carbohydrates (energy), proteins (growth and repair), fats (stored energy), vitamins, minerals, fibre and water. Exercise strengthens the heart; smoking damages the lungs.

workedExamples.question: Explain why pulse rate rises during exercise.
steps: Muscles work harder and need more oxygen and glucose.
The heart beats faster to deliver more blood.
workedExamples.answer: More blood carries more oxygen to working muscles.

commonMistakes: Mixing up arteries and veins.
Thinking the large intestine absorbs most food.
Saying the heart “makes” oxygen.
lessons.examTip: For “explain” questions, link cause and effect: “…because the muscles need more oxygen”.

lessons.title: Plants
lessons.keyIdea: Plants make their own food using light. Each part of the plant has a job.

sections.heading: Parts and functions
sections.body: Roots absorb water and minerals and anchor the plant. The stem supports it and carries water. Leaves use light to make food. Flowers make seeds.

sections.heading: Life cycle
sections.body: Pollination (pollen moves from anther to stigma) → fertilisation → seed formation → seed dispersal (wind, animals, water, explosion) → germination (needs water, warmth and air).

sections.heading: Growth
sections.body: Plants need light, water, warmth, air and nutrients. Without light, leaves turn yellow and the plant becomes weak.

workedExamples.question: Why are dandelion seeds light and fluffy?
steps: The fluff acts like a parachute.
Wind carries the seed far away.
Seedlings then do not compete with the parent.

commonMistakes: Saying seeds need light to germinate.
Confusing pollination with seed dispersal.
Thinking plants get their food from the soil.
lessons.examTip: Learn the difference between germination, pollination and dispersal — they are often tested together.

lessons.title: Living things and environments
lessons.keyIdea: Energy passes along food chains, and living things are adapted to where they live.

sections.heading: Food chains
sections.body: Every chain starts with a producer (a green plant). Arrows point from the food to the eater, showing the flow of energy. Herbivores eat plants; carnivores eat animals; omnivores eat both.

sections.heading: Changes in a chain
sections.body: If one population changes, others are affected. Fewer foxes → more rabbits → less grass.

sections.heading: Classification and adaptation
sections.body: Keys use yes/no questions to identify organisms. Adaptations are features that help survival: thick fur, camouflage, spines to save water.

workedExamples.question: In grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, what happens if frogs are removed?
steps: Grasshoppers have fewer predators, so they increase.
More grasshoppers eat more grass, so grass decreases.
Snakes have less food, so they decrease.
workedExamples.answer: Grasshoppers up, grass down, snakes down

commonMistakes: Drawing arrows from eater to food.
Saying the Sun is a producer.
Describing only one effect of a change instead of following the chain.
lessons.examTip: For “predict” questions, follow the chain one step at a time in both directions.

lessons.title: Materials and states of matter
lessons.keyIdea: Solids, liquids and gases are made of particles. Heating and cooling change the state.

sections.heading: The particle model
sections.body: Solid: close, fixed pattern, vibrate. Liquid: close, can move past each other, takes the shape of its container. Gas: far apart, move fast in all directions, fills its container.

sections.heading: Changes of state
sections.body: Melting (solid → liquid), freezing (liquid → solid), evaporating/boiling (liquid → gas), condensing (gas → liquid). Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.

sections.heading: Properties and uses
sections.body: Choose materials by property: copper conducts electricity (wires), plastic and wood are insulators (handles), glass is transparent (windows).

workedExamples.question: Explain why a cold can gets wet on the outside.
steps: Air contains water vapour.
It cools on the cold surface.
It condenses into liquid droplets.
workedExamples.answer: Condensation of water vapour from the air

commonMistakes: Thinking water on a cold glass leaked through.
Confusing evaporation with boiling (evaporation happens at any temperature).
Saying particles in a solid do not move at all.
lessons.examTip: Use the key words (evaporate, condense) — they are often what earns the mark.

lessons.title: Mixtures and changes
lessons.keyIdea: Some changes can be reversed; others make new materials. Mixtures can be separated using differences in properties.

sections.heading: Dissolving
sections.body: A soluble solid (sugar, salt) breaks into tiny particles spread through the liquid to make a solution. It has not disappeared. Warm water, stirring and smaller grains make it dissolve faster.

sections.heading: Separating mixtures
sections.body: Sieving: different-sized solids. Filtering: insoluble solid from a liquid. Evaporating: dissolved solid from a liquid. Magnet: magnetic materials such as iron.

sections.heading: Reversible and irreversible
sections.body: Melting, freezing and dissolving are reversible. Burning, cooking, rusting and mixing vinegar with bicarbonate of soda make new materials — they are irreversible.

workedExamples.question: How would you separate sand, salt and water?
steps: Filter: sand stays on the filter paper.
Evaporate the salty water that passed through.
Salt crystals are left behind.

commonMistakes: Saying salt can be filtered out of salt water.
Saying dissolving is the same as melting.
Calling cooking reversible.
lessons.examTip: Name the equipment and explain why it works: “filter paper lets water through but traps sand grains”.

lessons.title: Forces and motion
lessons.keyIdea: Forces are pushes and pulls, measured in newtons. Balanced forces mean no change in motion.

sections.heading: Types of force
sections.body: Gravity pulls objects towards Earth. Friction acts between surfaces and opposes motion. Air resistance and water resistance slow moving objects. Upthrust pushes up on objects in water.

sections.heading: Balanced and unbalanced
sections.body: Balanced forces: the object stays still or keeps moving at a steady speed. Unbalanced forces: it speeds up, slows down or changes direction.

sections.heading: Mass and weight
sections.body: Mass is the amount of matter (kg) and stays the same everywhere. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass (N) — it is less on the Moon.

workedExamples.question: A rock weighs 20 N in air and 14 N in water. What is the upthrust?
steps: Upthrust reduces the reading.

commonMistakes: Measuring force in kilograms.
Saying a moving object at steady speed has no forces on it.
Thinking mass changes on the Moon.
lessons.examTip: Draw force arrows: the longer arrow shows the bigger force and the direction of change.

lessons.title: Electricity and magnetism
lessons.keyIdea: Current flows only around a complete circuit. More cells make lamps brighter; more lamps in series make them dimmer.

sections.heading: Circuits
sections.body: A circuit needs a complete loop from one end of the cell to the other. A switch opens (breaks) or closes (completes) the loop. Use standard symbols in diagrams.

sections.heading: Changing a circuit
sections.body: Adding cells → brighter lamps, faster motors. Adding lamps in series → dimmer lamps. Longer or thinner wires → dimmer lamps.

sections.heading: Conductors and magnets
sections.body: Metals conduct electricity; plastic, wood, rubber and glass are insulators. Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic — aluminium and copper are not. Like poles repel, opposite poles attract.

workedExamples.question: Predict what happens when a third lamp is added in series.
steps: The same cell pushes current through more lamps.
Resistance goes up, current goes down.

commonMistakes: Saying all metals are magnetic.
Thinking one lamp goes out but the other stays lit in a series circuit.
Leaving gaps in circuit drawings.
lessons.examTip: In “predict” questions, give the change AND the reason.

lessons.title: Light and sound
lessons.keyIdea: Light travels in straight lines and we see objects when reflected light enters our eyes. Sounds are vibrations.

sections.heading: Seeing and shadows
sections.body: Light comes from a source (Sun, lamp, flame), reflects off objects and enters the eye. Opaque objects block light, making shadows. Moving the object closer to the light makes the shadow bigger.

sections.heading: Reflection and refraction
sections.body: Mirrors reflect light. Refraction is when light changes direction moving between materials, which makes a straw look bent in water.

sections.heading: Sound
sections.body: Sounds are made by vibrations passed through solids, liquids and gases (not a vacuum). Bigger vibrations → louder. Faster vibrations → higher pitch (shorter, tighter or thinner strings).

workedExamples.question: Why is a shadow the same shape as the object?
steps: Light travels in straight lines.
The object blocks the light that hits it.
The outline of the blocked area matches the object.

commonMistakes: Saying light travels from the eyes.
Calling the Moon a light source.
Mixing up pitch (high/low) with volume (loud/quiet).
lessons.examTip: Draw arrows on light ray diagrams — direction matters.

lessons.title: Earth and space
lessons.keyIdea: Earth spins on its axis (day and night) and orbits the Sun (a year). Its tilt causes the seasons.

sections.heading: Day, night and seasons
sections.body: Earth rotates once every 24 hours. It orbits the Sun once every 365¼ days. The tilt of its axis means each hemisphere gets more direct sunlight at different times — summer and winter.

sections.heading: The Moon and solar system
sections.body: The Moon orbits Earth about every 28 days; we see different amounts of its sunlit half (phases). Eight planets orbit the Sun, starting with Mercury.

sections.heading: Rocks and the Earth
sections.body: Igneous rock forms from cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary rock forms in layers and may contain fossils. Metamorphic rock is changed by heat and pressure. Earth has a crust, mantle and core; earthquakes and volcanoes happen where plates meet.

workedExamples.question: Why does the Sun appear to move across the sky?
steps: The Sun is not moving around Earth.
Earth rotates from west to east.
So the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west.

commonMistakes: Saying the seasons are caused by distance from the Sun.
Saying the Earth’s shadow causes the Moon’s phases.
Confusing rotation (a day) with orbit (a year).

lessons.title: Planning investigations and variables
lessons.keyIdea: Change one variable, measure one variable, and keep everything else the same.

sections.heading: Variables
sections.body: The independent variable is what you change. The dependent variable is what you measure. Control variables are kept the same to make the test fair.

sections.heading: Predictions
sections.body: A good prediction states the relationship and gives a reason: “The higher the ramp, the further the car will go, because it will be moving faster at the bottom.”

sections.heading: Equipment, repeats and safety
sections.body: Choose equipment that measures accurately (measuring cylinder for volume, stopwatch for time, forcemeter for force). Repeat measurements to spot anomalies. Identify risks and how to reduce them.

workedExamples.question: Plan a fair test: does water temperature affect how fast sugar dissolves?
steps: Change: water temperature.
Measure: time to dissolve.
Keep the same: volume of water, amount and type of sugar, stirring.
workedExamples.answer: Change one thing, measure one thing, control the rest

commonMistakes: Mixing up independent and dependent variables.
Changing two things at once.
Writing a prediction with no reason.
lessons.examTip: Remember: I change it (Independent), it Depends on what I change (Dependent).

lessons.title: Observations, data and conclusions
lessons.keyIdea: Look for the pattern, check for anomalies, and say what the evidence shows — no more.

sections.heading: Tables and graphs
sections.body: Put the independent variable in the first column and on the x-axis. Use a line graph for continuous data that changes over time or with another measured variable, and a bar chart for categories.

sections.heading: Patterns and anomalies
sections.body: Describe patterns using both variables: “As temperature increases, the time to dissolve decreases.” An anomalous result does not fit the pattern — repeat it.

sections.heading: Conclusions and improvements
sections.body: A conclusion answers the question using the data. Results are more reliable when there are more samples and repeats.

workedExamples.question: Results: 20 °C → 120 s, 40 °C → 75 s, 60 °C → 42 s. Describe the pattern.
steps: Look at both columns together.
Temperature goes up while time goes down.
workedExamples.answer: As temperature increases, dissolving time decreases.

commonMistakes: Describing only one variable (“the time goes down”).
Drawing conclusions from one result.
Including anomalous results in a mean without checking them.
lessons.examTip: When reading values from a graph, use a ruler and go up and across carefully.
